facts.statement: Connectors in different data groups cannot be used together in one app or flow. Connectors in the same group can.
Microsoft advises classifying connectors that host business data as Business and those that host personal-use data as Non-Business.
The names Business and Non-Business are only labels. What matters is which connectors share a group.
Microsoft advises keeping Non-Business as the default group, then moving new connectors to Business or Blocked after evaluating them.
A published list of Microsoft connectors cannot be blocked with classic data policies. They can only be classified as Business or Non-Business.
All third-party connectors can be blocked. All Microsoft-owned premium connectors can be blocked except Dataverse.

Child flows share an internal dependency with the HTTP connector, so its grouping can affect child flows. Microsoft suggests Non-Business or Blocked in shared environments, with dedicated environments and a restricted maker list for those who need it.
The Content Conversion connector is not available for classification through data policies.
Tenant admins classify custom connectors by host URL pattern. Environment admins classify them by name. A custom connector with no specific rule falls to the default group.
For shared productivity environments, Microsoft recommends a policy limited to Microsoft 365 and other standard microservices that blocks everything else, and that also applies to new environments.
Microsoft recommends more permissive policies for chosen team environments, which could allow connectors such as Azure services.
For production environments, Microsoft recommends excluding them from the shared policies and working with the business unit to establish which connectors and combinations they use.
Microsoft recommends a minimal number of policies per environment, managed centrally at tenant level, because all applicable policies are evaluated together.
When several policies apply to an environment, the most restrictive result is imposed. Environment policies cannot override tenant-wide policies.
Different Business and Non-Business choices across policies are combined, and the most restrictive grouping is imposed.
Data policies know the connector, but not the connection. They cannot tell whether a connector points at a development, test or production system.
Data policies apply at environment or tenant level, never at user level.
Microsoft describes three ways to handle an exception, including denying it or creating a use-case-specific policy for the excluded environment.
Limiting a connector or its actions affects makers and also apps, flows and agents that already exist.
A connection is a saved credential, stored in the environment that hosts the app or flow.
The publisher of a connector can differ from the owner of the service. Microsoft can publish the Salesforce connector while Salesforce owns the service.

Connector action control allows or blocks individual actions and triggers on blockable connectors. It is not available for unblockable or custom connectors. A default setting decides how future actions are treated.
Allowing or blocking individual triggers is currently available only through PowerShell.

Endpoint filtering lets admins control which endpoints makers can connect to. It is available only for HTTP, HTTP with Microsoft Entra ID, HTTP Webhook, SQL Server, Azure Blob Storage, SMTP, Browser Automation and UI Automation.
Endpoint filtering evaluates static endpoints only. It does not apply to environment variables, custom inputs or endpoints created at runtime.
Endpoint filtering is a preview feature, and Microsoft states that preview features are not meant for production use.
Advanced connector policies (ACP) use a strict allowlist. Every connector and action is blocked unless allowed.
Under ACP, new connectors added to the platform are blocked automatically.
ACP covers certified connectors and MCP connectors. Custom and HTTP connectors are not yet supported, and virtual connectors will not be.
On non-managed environments, nonblockable connectors stay nonblockable under ACP. On Managed Environments, any connector or action can be blocked.
In mixed mode, ACP runs alongside classic data policies and the most restrictive settings from both are enforced. Microsoft recommends this while migrating.
In ACP-only mode, classic data policies are ignored for that scope but not deleted.
Mixed mode lets classic data policies provide action control and endpoint filtering until those features are native to ACP.
ACP enforces the allowlist as soon as it is saved or published, so the allowed list must be curated first.
ACP does not carry forward the Business and Non-Business categories, so allowed connectors are not separated from each other.
An ACP policy holds a ConnectorManagement rule set with an AllowedConnectorList. Each entry names the connector and how its actions and connection types are governed.
ACP can block an MCP server as a whole. Control over individual MCP tools is not available.
Power Platform tenant isolation only works for connectors that use Microsoft Entra ID-based authentication.
A known issue means tenant isolation is not enforced for connections made with the Azure DevOps connector.
Azure Logic Apps connector use is blocked through Azure Policy, which is a separate control from Power Platform data policies.
A desktop flow that violates a data policy is marked as suspended and cannot be run.
Data policies govern Copilot Studio agents, including sign-in requirements, HTTP requests, publishing channels, skills and the use of connectors as tools.
With a Shareable authentication type, the connection is shared when a Power App is shared with another user.
NIST describes semi-quantitative assessment as using bins, scales or representative numbers whose values and meanings do not carry over to other contexts.
Cox shows that risk matrices can give identical ratings to very different risks and can rate smaller risks above larger ones.
OWASP lists authorization misuse among the top risks of citizen development, including credentials that are shared across applications.
